ranking: 1. Buy and hold a low-cost S&P 500 fund (VOO/IVV, or SPY; VOO/IVV add only +0.03-0.04 pp/yr). Never sell, keep adding new money, and plan to end the position by donating appreciated lots or holding to a step-up at death. This is the only choice that meets the user's 'good confidence' bar, because its excess is about zero by construction. In CA no challenger passes that bar under any way the position can end.

2. If the user insists on a bet: keep at least 75% in an S&P core that is never sold, plus a small leveraged-trend sleeve (r2_combos A1/A3 form). Drawdowns were at or below SPY's in every history, the step-up penalty was small because the core is never sold, and the expected excess is about +1.5-2 pp/yr (grid median). It still has holdout p 0.12-0.30, DSR <= 0.04, a ~21% bootstrap chance of trailing SPY at 20 years, and lag-1 removes its 1986+ significance. The site cannot run it as a single preset.

3. The website's 'Beat the S&P: 2x trend (CA)' preset, all-in (SSO when SPY is >3% above SMA175, IEF when >3% below, daily at the close). It has the highest backtested excess at survivable drawdown. On real SSO 2006-26 in CA: score +4.48, full +3.67, boot p 0.116 (bootstrap CI about -1.0 to +7.8 pp/yr), max DD -48% vs -55%, and a Sharpe of 0.67 vs SPY's 0.65, so the excess is leverage rather than skill. Its weaknesses: SMA175/3% was chosen after the fact (DSR 0.002-0.006), its excess since 2010 is about zero, its whipsaw years are deep, it depends on executing at the same close, and it loses its significance when the position ends in a step-up or a gift. The pre-registered twin (SMA200/3% + 60-day short-term deferral) is essentially tied and is not on the site.

4. The website's 'Beat the S&P (CA)' tax-managed momentum preset. Its expected edge is about zero: score +0.66, it fails item 2, DSR 0.009, the 1986-2026 twin is negative (full -0.19, p 0.54), and the lead comes from QQQ/XLK in the menu. The book freezes into 50-60% growth/tech with 81-87% unrealized gains, and a replayed 2000-02 tech bust loses -56% to -71% vs SPY's -47.5%. That is concentration risk with no expected pay for it.
5. The 3x leveraged trend (UPRO/IEF, SMA175 or SMA200). Rejected: -88% to -93% in 1929-35, a 17-24% chance of an 80%+ drawdown within 20 years, and a one-day lag gives -76% in 1987.
6. Everything else (unlevered SPY timing, TAA, seasonality, dip/VIX, macro/curve, factor switches, global, sector rotation, stock picking, harvesting structures). All fail after CA tax.
pick: Just buy and hold an S&P 500 index fund (VOO or IVV; SPY is fine) in the taxable account, never sell it, and plan to end the position by donating appreciated lots or holding to a step-up. Do not follow either 'Beat the S&P' preset with the core of the account. If the user knowingly wants the leverage bet, cap it at a satellite of 20-25% or less beside a never-sold S&P core.
expected_excess_after_ca_tax:
The pick: 0.00 to +0.04 pp/yr vs SPY, by construction (VOO/IVV's lower fees add +0.03-0.04). Under a step-up or donation ending, buy-and-hold also gains relative to every realizing strategy.

The best challenger, the website's 2x trend preset (all-in), honestly: about +0.5 to +2 pp/yr expected after CA tax, central about +1. A given 20-year outcome could plausibly fall anywhere from about -3 to +5 pp/yr. The chance of trailing SPY at 20 years is about 25% (strategy-level bootstrap) to 60% (market-path bootstrap with 1-3 months of trend persistence).

How the range was built:
- Headline (first start): +3.7 to +3.8 full excess (2000-26 engine; real SSO 2006-26).
- Averaged over start dates, that falls to +1.6 (2000-26) and +2.3 (1986-26) for the pre-registered pick.
- The 1930-85 holdout gives full +2.5 / score +3.3 (p 0.16), but it is not significant.
- A step-up or donation ending takes off another 0.7-1.1 pp/yr (p rises to 0.20-0.29; worst 10-year window -1.5 to -1.8).
- The post-2010 decades were +0.6 and -0.3.
- Financing costs more now than in the near-zero-rate SSO era. The synthetic was about 0.55 pp/yr too cheap when T-bills were above 2%.
- Multiple-testing shrinkage applies after ~14,000 configs (DSR 0.002-0.006).

For the never-sold core + 25% sleeve, the whole account gets about +0.3 to +0.6 pp/yr.
caveats: Buy-and-hold is chosen because it is the only option that meets the user's 'good confidence' standard, not because it is expected to outperform. The 2x trend rule had positive after-tax excess in every history tested (2000-26, 1986-26, 1930-85), so buy-and-hold may well trail it over the next 20 years. The choice trades an uncertain, fat-tailed premium for certainty of the benchmark.

Buy-and-hold still carries full equity risk: -55% in 2007-09 and -81% to -84% in 1929-32. None of this research removes that. It has to be handled by overall asset allocation and an emergency fund, not by this account's strategy.

The 2x trend edge comes from a few slow bear markets (1929-32, 1973-74, 2000-02, 2007-09). Ten-year after-tax excess was +0.6 pp/yr in the 2010s and -0.3 in 2020-26. Pre-tax it trailed SPY in 13 of 26 calendar years, by 15-24 pp in 2011, 2015, 2016, 2020 and 2022. For start dates 2010-23 the SMA175 baseline's to-the-end excess averaged -0.47 pp/yr and was negative in 47% of them. The 100% 10-year beat rate on real SSO comes from 41 heavily overlapping windows, most of which contain 2008.

Behavioural survivability is poor. In fast corrections it loses more than the index: 2022 -37% to -41% vs -24%; 2015-16 -38% vs -13%; 1998 -36% vs -19%; 2011 -30% vs -19%. It then often re-enters late. Investors tend to quit in exactly those years, which locks in the whipsaw losses and misses the slow-bear payoff, which is where all of the edge lives.

Tail risk is real. A single -20% day while invested takes about 40% of the account at that close (roughly 5-7% odds over 20 years). From a 1929 start it still fell -77% by 1932. On 1930-85 windows the max DD was -67% to -73%. In the market-path bootstrap its median max DD is -59% to -66% (SPY -43% to -49%), and the chance of an 80% drawdown within 20 years is 5-11%. A 2x daily-reset fund would be wiped out by a -50% index day.

Execution is fragile. The rule must trade at the same day's close with a market-on-close order, deciding at about 3:45 pm ET (12:45 pm PT) every trading day for decades. One day late in October 1987 turns the escape into a -59% drawdown (1986-2026 p 0.26). Weekly checks fail. Missed days from vacations, illness or broker outages are a real risk.

Leveraged-ETF mechanics: SSO is a swap-based daily-reset fund with about a 0.9% expense ratio, financing at T-bills plus a spread, and volatility drag. Its distributions are ordinary income (4-5% of value in 2006-07; such a year can cost about 2 pp). There is counterparty risk and a small risk the fund closes, which would force a sale. The real-SSO record, 2006-26, includes about 10 years of near-zero rates, which flatters the leverage premium compared with today's.
The IEF off-leg relied on the 1982-2020 bond bull market. With T-bills as the safe asset, p is 0.14-0.20. In 2022 stocks and Treasuries fell together.

Tax issues the engine understates for the trend rule: it pays tax as it goes ($411k paid on a $100k start, real SSO 2006-26, vs $0 for SPY), so it loses deferral. The engine uses flat 48.1%/28.1% rates, but lumpy realizations in a large account can reach CA's 10.3-11.3% brackets and the federal 20% long-term / 37% short-term brackets, which buy-and-hold never triggers. Under a step-up or donation ending, none of the 54 2x neighbourhood configs passes bar items 1-3 in any history.

The 2x preset's parameters were chosen after the fact. SMA175/3% is the best point in its neighbourhood. On real SSO, SMA200/4% scores +2.4 (p 0.21, worst 10-year window -1.37), and SMA200 vs SMA175 moves sub-samples by about 1.5 pp/yr. Parameter selection inside the 2x structure has no out-of-sample skill on 1930-85 (PBO 0.60-0.82).

The 'Beat the S&P (CA)' momentum preset should not be used as a core holding. Its lead depends on QQQ/XLK being in the menu and on the start date, 5-year windows starting in 2020-21 lost 2.8-4.8 pp/yr, and its book cannot be de-risked without a large tax bill.

Several round-2 agents (Section 1256 futures, CAPE, options overlays, final rotation test, other markets) had not reported when this was written, and the r2_gap5 HIFO report was still pending its verdict. The recommendation should change only if one of them passes the full bar on data not used to find it. Nothing reviewed so far did.

Outside the engine, buy-and-hold can be improved slightly: tax-loss harvesting by swapping to a similar but not substantially identical index fund in drawdowns (about +0.2 pp/yr from offsetting other gains and the $3k ordinary-income deduction), avoiding wash sales with dividend reinvestment and IRA purchases, and donating the lowest-basis lots.
what_to_tell_the_user: After testing about 14,000 strategies, nothing beat simply buying and holding an S&P 500 fund after California taxes with the confidence you asked for. My recommendation is to buy a low-cost S&P 500 fund (VOO or IVV), keep adding to it, and never sell it. If you eventually give the shares to charity or leave them to heirs, the gains are never taxed, which makes buy-and-hold even harder to beat. The best challenger is the website's 'Beat the S&P: 2x trend (CA)' preset. It did come out ahead in every history tested, but nearly all of that came from sidestepping a few slow bear markets (the 1930s, 1973-74, 2000-02, 2008), and since 2010 it has added roughly nothing after tax. It also has to be traded at the closing price on the exact day the signal changes, for decades: acting one day late in October 1987 turned a clean escape into a 59% loss. In fast sell-offs it loses more than the market, for example about -40% in 2022 when the S&P fell about 24%. A single 20%-down day while it is invested would take about 40% of the account at once. A realistic expectation is perhaps +0.5 to +2 percentage points a year after tax, with roughly a 1-in-4 to 1-in-2 chance of being behind the S&P after 20 years. The older 'Beat the S&P (CA)' momentum preset has an expected edge near zero and slowly turns into a concentrated tech bet you can't unwind without a big tax bill. If you still want the leveraged bet, keep it to a small side portion (20-25% at most) next to an S&P core you never sell. Follow its rules exactly, and decide in advance that you will stick with it through years when it trails by 15-20 points.
reasoning:
This judgment looks at the downside. The question is whether any candidate earns a positive expected excess with 'good confidence', meaning it survives realistic endings, execution slips, tails and the investor's own behaviour. None does.

(1) Statistics. Every leveraged candidate has DSR 0.002-0.006 after ~14,000 trials.
- r2_lev2x's pre-registered 96-design grid has its pick failing the 1930-85 holdout (p 0.164). No design passing the hard filters gets a holdout p of 0.10 or lower.
- Averaged over start dates, p is 0.35 (2000-26) and 0.25 (1986-26), and the excess is +1.6 and +2.3, against the first-start +3.8 and +3.2.
- The website preset on real SSO (2006-26, CA) has p 0.116, a bootstrap CI that spans zero (about -1.0 to +7.8 pp/yr), and a Sharpe of 0.67 vs 0.65: the excess is leverage, not skill.
- The SMA175/3% parameter is the after-the-fact best point. SMA200/4% on the same real data gives +2.39, p 0.21 and a negative worst 10-year window.

(2) Endings. r2_gap4 shows that a CA investor who holds to a step-up or donates loses 0.7-1.1 pp/yr of the 2x edge. p doubles to 0.20-0.29, the worst 10-year window turns negative, and no 2x neighbourhood config passes items 1-3 in any history. A 20-year retirement sale also pushes p to 0.11-0.12. The engine's flat rates also ignore bracket creep from lumpy realizations, which only hurts the realizing strategy.

(3) Regime dependence. The edge comes entirely from slow bears: 2010s +0.6, 2020-26 -0.3, and for 2010-23 starts the SMA175 baseline averaged -0.47 to the end, negative in 47%. With 1-3 months of trend persistence the market-path bootstrap trails SPY in 57-66% of 20-year paths.

(4) Tails and mechanics:
- Execution must be at the same close: a one-day lag gives -59% in 1987 and p 0.26.
- One -20% day while invested costs about 40% of the account.
- 1929-32 still fell -77%.
- The market-path median DD is -59% to -66% vs SPY's -43% to -49%.
- SSO's financing and ordinary-income distributions, the IEF bond-bull dependence, and the near-zero-rate SSO era all make forward returns lower than in-sample.

(5) Behaviour. Pre-tax it trailed SPY in 13 of 26 calendar years, by 15-24 pp in five of them, and lost -37% to -41% in 2022 vs -24%. Those are the years investors abandon a rule, and they come before the rare payoff years.

(6) Momentum preset. Its expected edge is about zero (fails item 2, DSR 0.009, 1986+ twin negative). It carries uncompensated concentration and frozen-book risk (-56% to -71% in a replayed tech bust).

So buy-and-hold is the high-confidence answer to the question the user actually asked. The 2x trend is a legitimate but low-confidence, fat-tailed expected-value bet. It is best limited to a never-sold-core satellite, where drawdowns stay at or below SPY's but the whole-account benefit shrinks to about +0.3 to +0.6 pp/yr. 'High' confidence refers to the decision (nothing meets the bar, so default to buy-and-hold), not to buy-and-hold outperforming the 2x rule.
